claims.text: The starting W–Cu composite contains discrete W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix.
The untreated W–Cu composite is prone to phase separation and interfacial void formation under service conditions.
Rapid liquid-phase-assisted ultrahigh-temperature sintering can induce a transient eutectic liquid at W–Cu interfaces.
Controlled cooling after transient-liquid formation can produce a bridging interfacial phase.
The solidified W–Cu interfacial phase may be an intermetallic or transition layer.
The transient eutectic liquid homogenizes the W–Cu interface.
The transient liquid fills interfacial voids.
The transient liquid reduces W–Cu interfacial energy.
A solidified interfacial phase improves adhesion between composite components.
The solidified interfacial phase limits subsequent phase separation.
The solidified interfacial phase limits interfacial void formation.
Improved interfacial integrity creates more continuous thermal-conduction paths through the W–Cu composite.
The treated W–Cu composite will have higher thermal conductivity than a conventionally sintered untreated control.
The thermal-conductivity improvement will persist under simultaneous high heat-transfer and irradiation exposure.
Conventionally sintered W–Cu displays considerable phase separation and interfacial voiding under service conditions.
Rapid ultrahigh-temperature processing is an applicable regime for implementing the proposed transient-liquid intervention.
The intervention will remain effective over relevant temperature and radiation exposures if the induced interfacial phase remains stable.
The optimal temperature, duration, and cooling rate for producing the proposed W–Cu transient eutectic remain to be established.
The long-term stability of the induced interfacial phase under irradiation and thermal cycling is uncertain.
